desc:
The string s contains round brackets ( and ) and lowercase letters. A string is valid when its brackets are balanced: scanning from left to right, a ) never appears when no ( is waiting, and at the end no ( is left over. Letters do not matter.

You may delete brackets (never letters) until the string becomes valid, and you want to delete as few brackets as possible. Return the number of different strings that can result from a deletion of that minimal size. Two results are different if the resulting texts differ.

Example: s = "()())()" needs one deletion and can become "(())()" or "()()()", so the answer is 2. For ")(" both brackets must go and the only result is the empty string, so the answer is 1.
constraints: s consists of the characters ( ) and a-z
hints: First find out how many closing and opening brackets have to be deleted at least. A left-to-right scan with a balance counter tells you.
Search over which brackets to delete, but only delete as many as the minimum. Different deletions can produce the same text, so you need a rule against duplicates.

When several equal brackets stand in a row, deleting any one of them gives the same text. Allow only the first bracket of such a run to be deleted, and delete positions in increasing order so that each text is generated once.
editorial: Scan left to right keeping a balance. Whenever the balance would go below zero there is a surplus ) in the prefix; at least one of the closing brackets seen so far must be deleted. After the scan, the balance that is left is the number of surplus (, which are handled by running the same logic on the reversed string with the roles of the brackets swapped.

The classic recursion fixes the first scan position i where the balance becomes negative and tries to remove one ) at some position j ≤ i. To avoid duplicates it removes s[j] only if it is the first ) of its run of equal characters, and the next level only looks at positions from j on. When the scan has no more violations the string is reversed and processed again for the opening brackets. Every string that reaches the end is a distinct, minimal and valid result, so the answer is the number of such strings. With at most 20 characters the search is small.
time: O(2<sup>n</sup>) worst case, much less with pruning
